newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu lawyer sees no chance of criminal charges.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu lawyer sees no chance of criminal charges.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu's lawyer said on Monday there was "no chance" the Israeli prime minister, questioned by police over alleged government corruption, would face criminal charges.
Lawyer Yaacov Weinroth, hired by the prime minister on Saturday, said Netanyahu had done no wrong in connection with the ill-fated appointment of an attorney-general last month.

"After studying the facts regarding the prime minister, it is my clear opinion that he was not involved in any misconduct," Weinroth told Reuters. "It will be found out that the allegations against the prime minister are baseless."
As for the outcome of the investigation, he said: "There is no chance in the world that there will be an indictment against the prime minister."

Police said on Monday Supreme Court Chief Justice Aharon Barak gave a statement to investigators. More than 20 people, including the prime minister, cabinet ministers, lawyers and journalists, have been questioned in the case in the last month.

Netanyahu himself called for a "thorough investigation" into allegations on Israel Television on January 22 that the short-lived appointment of Roni Bar-On as attorney-general earlier that month was part of a shady deal with a politician on trial on corruption charges.
Bar-On, an activist in Netanyahu's Likud party, resigned after only twelve hours in office.
The television suggested the appointment was not only bad judgment but also criminal.

It alleged that Shas party leader Aryeh Deri, on trial on corruption charges for the past three years and a key figure in the ruling coalition, had pressed to have Bar-On named to the post to arrange a plea bargain.
Bowing to such alleged pressure would fall under the criminal charge of breach of public trust, legal experts say.

According to the report, Deri had demanded Bar-On get the attorney-general's job in exchange for Shas's support for Netanyahu's accord with the Palestinians on an Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron last month.
Weinroth, deflecting responsibility for the Bar-On appointment from Netanyahu to Justice Minister Tsahi Hanegbi, said the prime minister had simply accepted Hanegbi's recommendation of Bar-On.
Weinroth said Netanyahu took Hanegbi's word Justice Barak had approved Bar-On's candidacy.
"Tsahi Hanegbi was convinced that Supreme Court Chief Justice Barak had heard about the appointment and didn't have any objections," he said.

"This is what he (Hanegbi) said to the prime minister about an hour before the meeting for the appointment," he said, referring to a January cabinet meeting where Bar-On was appointed attorney-general.

Police questioned Netanyahu for four hours last Tuesday. Weinroth confirmed the prime minister had been interrogated "under caution" -- a warning police use before questioning people when they believe charges might be filed against them.
Weinroth blasted the police's handling of the investigation, charging interrogators with leaking information to the media.

"We don't think that every newspaper has to know different information about what's going on inside the interrogation," he said. "It's something against the basic right of any person interrogated. It's against Israeli law by the way as well."
Chief Police Investigator Sando Mazor on Monday denied the existence of police leaks.
